settings.prompt:
Autonomously review this Java source repository for potential security
vulnerabilities using the available read-only tools. Do not ask the user questions or summarize
tool output. Copy exact relative paths from list_files or index results; never invent or prefix a path.
A file listing or index hint is only navigation; inspect original source and seek
counter-evidence before deciding. Trace plausible untrusted input to security-sensitive
operations where possible, and check relevant guards and configuration. Report at most 10
candidates supported by exact source lines, with root cause, preconditions, counter-evidence,
and missing evidence. Do not assume a vulnerability exists. If source review finds no supported
candidate, submit an empty candidate list. Your final action must be submit_findings; natural
language commentary is not a report. Do not use project names, dataset identifiers, or a guessed
known answer as evidence.

counter_evidence: Attribute values are produced by the tokeniser, which decodes entities; if javascript: is already decoded to javascript: the startsWith check would reject it
The Attribute constructor trims/lowercases only the key, not the value, so case is handled by toLowerCase() at the comparison site
Values whose absUrl() is non-empty are validated against the resolved absolute URL rather than the raw string
candidates.description: Whitelist.testValidProtocol resolves the URL attribute via el.absUrl(attr.getKey()); when that returns an empty string it substitutes the raw attribute value ("if it could not be made abs, run as-is to allow custom unknown protocols") and then only performs a lowercase startsWith("protocol:") check against the configured protocol set (lines 523-540). No normalization of HTML entities, embedded control characters, or whitespace occurs inside this method before the comparison. The accepted value therefore depends on whether the parser stored an entity-encoded or otherwise obfuscated value, and the gate can be decided against a never-resolved raw string. Source alone does not show what normalization the tokeniser already applied to attribute values, so the effective strength of this gate cannot be confirmed from this method in isolation.
missing_evidence: Tokeniser/TokeniserState handling of HTML entities and control characters inside attribute values (not traced)
Whether Element.absUrl() can return empty for values a browser would still treat as a scheme (StringUtil.resolve/URL resolution not traced)
An end-to-end cleaning test with obfuscated scheme values in the frozen repository
preconditions: Application cleans untrusted HTML with a whitelist that allows a URL-bearing attribute (e.g. a[href] in basic()/relaxed())
The attribute value cannot be resolved to an absolute URL (e.g. no/invalid base URI, relative-looking value), so absUrl() returns empty
The raw stored value passes the lowercase startsWith("<allowed>:") comparison while still being interpreted as a dangerous scheme downstream
candidates.title: Protocol validation falls back to the raw attribute value when absUrl() is empty

counter_evidence: Cleaner.isValid creates a shell document and runs the visitor over the original body, so the observable mutation is on the caller's original Document
The documented contract of clean() states the original document is not modified; isValid() makes no such promise
testValidProtocol is private and reached only through isSafeAttribute
candidates.description: Inside testValidProtocol, when preserveRelativeLinks is false the attribute value is overwritten with the resolved value (attr.setValue(value)) before the protocol loop decides whether the attribute is safe. This side effect occurs inside a predicate whose name implies validation. A caller that checks safety without cloning the element (e.g. Cleaner.isValid, which runs copySafeNodes over the original document) can observe mutation of the original document's attributes even when the document is reported invalid.
missing_evidence: Whether callers rely on isValid() being non-mutating
Runtime behaviour of absUrl()/StringUtil.resolve for values used in tests
preconditions: Caller uses Cleaner.isValid on a document it does not want modified, or otherwise invokes isSafeAttribute/testValidProtocol on original nodes
preserveRelativeLinks is false (the default) and the attribute has a resolvable URL
candidates.title: testValidProtocol rewrites the attribute while checking safety

counter_evidence: Default whitelists (none/simpleText/basic/basicWithImages/relaxed) do not include script/style in their tag sets, so DataNode content under those parents would be dropped with the unsafe parent
NodeTraversor descent means the parent element itself must have passed isSafeTag in head for the destination to descend
candidates.description: In Cleaner.CleaningVisitor.head, DataNode content is copied into the cleaned output when whitelist.isSafeTag(source.parent().nodeName()) is true (Cleaner.java:103-106). The safety decision for the data payload is keyed off the incoming node's name string, not off the already-validated, normalized element actually accepted into the output. Combined with raw-data serialization of DataNode content (script/style style content), script/style text could be reproduced verbatim whenever the parent name happens to be whitelisted. Whether a whitelist can be configured (or already is, in default sets) such that the parent name is whitelisted while the element serializes as executable content was not verified in this pass.
missing_evidence: Whether Element.data()/DataNode is created for script/style content by the tokeniser and how it is serialized (Element.html/outerHtml not traced)
A concrete whitelist configuration combining a safe tag name with raw-data serialization
preconditions: A whitelist marks the parent tag name as safe while the element's content is treated as raw data by serializers
Attacker-controlled input can place DataNode content under such a parent
candidates.title: DataNode copy decision uses the parent nodeName rather than the sanitized element type

counter_evidence: Keys are trimmed and lowercased; only whitespace at the ends is removed, so interior content is still written verbatim
Documentation says keys are trimmed and normalized to lower case and that createFromEncoded assumes keys are simple word characters
Nodes produced from parsed HTML get keys via the tokeniser, which constrains key characters
candidates.description: Attribute.html writes the key directly into the accumulator (accum.append(key)) without running it through Entities.escape, while values are escaped. Keys are normalized only by trim().toLowerCase() and must be non-empty. If any code path can set an attribute key containing whitespace-separated sequences or angle-bracket/quote characters, the emitted markup can escape the attribute context. The parser produces keys from tokeniser state that restricts characters, so a route to inject such a key would require programmatic attribute creation or a tokeniser path not traced here.
missing_evidence: Whether any public API path allows constructing an Attribute from fully attacker-controlled raw key text that reaches html()
Serializer usage sites that treat attribute output as trusted HTML
preconditions: An attribute key containing characters meaningful in HTML (spaces, quotes, < or >) reaches serialization
The resulting string is consumed as HTML (e.g. stored/served or re-parsed)
candidates.title: Attribute keys are serialized without escaping

counter_evidence: Charset handling is guarded by support/name validation, limiting the accepted sets
The reviewed lines show no file/network access driven by the declared charset
candidates.description: DataUtil.parseByteData first decodes the byte buffer with an assumed/default charset, parses the input, then extracts a charset declared in the untrusted document (a meta http-equiv/content-type or meta[charset] element), and re-decodes the same byte buffer using the declared charset. Charset name resolution is bounded by Charset.isSupported / IllegalCharsetNameException guards on the reviewed paths. The concern is that the effective decoding of untrusted bytes is controlled by an in-document declaration; no arbitrary-charset-driven file or network access was found in the reviewed lines.
missing_evidence: Exact control flow of parseByteData between the allowed spans (DataUtil.java:1-120 and 120-225) was not fully followed end to end
Whether the first-pass decode can itself be influenced by the content before the meta element is seen
preconditions: Untrusted byte content is parsed through DataUtil.parseByteData
The document declares a charset that is supported by the runtime
candidates.title: Charset re-decode driven by an attacker-supplied meta charset in the document body

counter_evidence: The custom URL repair only affects the narrow "http:/x" form and reverts to normal parsing otherwise
Cookie values are not themselves validated (acknowledged in a todo comment for the request cookie string)
No evidence that redirects to arbitrary hosts are attacker-reachable in the intended usage
candidates.description: On a redirect, HttpConnection.Response.execute clears POST data, reads the Location header, performs a string-level repair for values beginning with "http:/", builds the next URL relative to the current request URL with encodeUrl(), then copies every response cookie into the next request and recursively follows. The cookie propagation is scheme/host agnostic: Set-Cookie values from one origin are attached to the redirected request target, without a SameSite/domain/origin comparison at this site. Where a redirect target is attacker-influenced (e.g. redirect to a different host), cookies collected from the previous response are forwarded to the new host.
missing_evidence: processResponseHeaders parsing of Set-Cookie truncates at the first ';' and ignores domain/path attributes, so cross-domain behavior should be traced further
Intended usage of the Connection API (library vs server-side outbound fetcher)
preconditions: The connection follows redirects (followRedirects default true)
The response sets cookies and a Location header pointing at a different origin the caller trusts for state
candidates.title: Redirect Location handling repairs a malformed scheme and forwards cookies to the redirected target

counter_evidence: The default is a secure value and is only set to false by an explicit caller-supplied boolean
The static sslSocketFactory is used only when the per-request flag is false
This mirrors a documented public API (Connection.validateTLSCertificates)
candidates.description: HttpConnection's connection setup checks the request's validateTLSCertificates flag and, when false, installs an all-trusting SSLSocketFactory and a HostnameVerifier whose verify() always returns true. The insecure factory is cached in a static field shared by all instances. The default is secure, so this is an explicit opt-out; however, if an application ever calls validateTLSCertificates(false) or exposes it to untrusted configuration, subsequent HTTPS connections through this code path accept any certificate and hostname, defeating impersonation protection.
missing_evidence: Any caller in this repository that passes false (integration tests were not fully reviewed)
Whether external configuration can reach this setter
preconditions: A code path calls Connection.validateTLSCertificates(false) / Request.validateTLSCertificates(false)
An HTTPS request is then executed through the same JVM
candidates.title: TLS certificate and hostname validation can be disabled, installing a cached all-trusting factory

counter_evidence: fromJsoup only calls newDocument() and convert(); no parse() of external input appears in the reviewed source
The class is explicitly labeled experimental
No attacker-controlled XML source is passed to the factory in the reviewed methods
candidates.description: W3CDom initializes a DocumentBuilderFactory with DocumentBuilderFactory.newInstance() and no security features, then creates a builder and a new Document via newDocumentBuilder(). The reviewed methods only create an empty document and populate it programmatically from a jsoup Document (fromJsoup/convert); parsing of external XML is not performed in those lines, so the typical XXE/DTD exposure of an unconfigured factory is not exercised here. The field is protected and the class is documented as experimental, so subclasses could change usage.
missing_evidence: Any subclass or other repository code that reuses W3CDom.factory for parsing untrusted XML
Whether downstream users treat this helper as an XML parsing entry point
preconditions: A subclass or extension calls factory.newDocumentBuilder().parse(...) on untrusted XML using the inherited, unconfigured factory
Or a caller supplies an external entity-expanding source through methods not present in this class
candidates.title: W3CDom holds an unhardened DocumentBuilderFactory
